catalog_locator: p. 83, sec. 1 'Introduction'; paper = pp. 83-89 of the 342-page whole-issue PDF of Studies in African Linguistics Supplement 9 (TOC: 'THE INTONATION SYSTEM OF ISOKO 83')
catalog_quote: Isoko is a Southwestern Edoid language spoken in the Isoko Local Government Area of the Bendel state of Nigeria. It is a discrete level tone language with two level tones: high (H) and low (L) as stated by Mafeni [1969] and Elugbe [1977]. Both previous writers, without any discussion, mention the possible use of intonation in Isoko. Though Mafeni claims the existence of downstep and downdrift, Isoko has neither. Moreover, the phenomenon of final low tone raising discussed by Elugbe is a feature of the intonation system. ... In addition to the H and L tones, contour tones also exist at the phonetic level. They are derived from underlying sequences of level tones: a segmental and a floating. ... The lexical function of tone is only prominent in the noun. The tone of the verb stem (Vs) is continually changing from one construction to another; our phonological analysis assigns no underlying tone to the Vs since there is evidence that it acquires its tone by polarisation.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Isoko (Uzere-based standard) is described as a two-level (H, L) register tone language without downstep/downdrift; final L is raised to mid in statements and citation forms (Elugbe 1977); lexical tone contrasts reside in nouns, verb stems get tone by polarisation. None of the opened primary descriptions (Donwa-Ifode 1985a, 1985b; Elugbe 1977) says anything about word stress or accent, and LAPSyD, compiled from Donwa 1982 and Mafeni 1969, explicitly records 'Stress: No mention'.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: Mafeni 1969 analysed a third 'downstepped high' level, which Elugbe 1977 and Donwa-Ifode reanalyse as predictable final-low raising.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone on words (nouns vs verb stems) and sentence-level intonation; citation forms show final-low raising. No word-level stress domain is defined by any source seen.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Uzere dialect / Uzere-based spoken standard of Isoko (glottocode isok1239; LAPSyD entry 'Isoko, Uzere dialect'). Donwa-Ifode = Shirley O. Donwa (1982 thesis) = Shirley Yul-Ifode (2022), the same native-speaker linguist.

sources.note: Nothing about stress/accent. States Isoko 'is a discrete level tone language with two level tones: high (H) and low (L)', no downstep or downdrift, contour tones derived; lexical tone prominent only in nouns, verb stems toneless underlyingly (polarisation); rest of paper is sentence intonation (five pitch levels, Low/High/Rising/Falling tunes).

sources.citation: Ilolo, Akpoghene O. 2013. Vowel reduction in Educated Isoko English. PhD thesis, Department of English, University of Ibadan.
sources.note: Second-hand summary of Isoko L1 phonology (secs 1.5-1.7, pp.19-25): vowels, syllable types V/CV/CCV/CCCV after Dunstan 1969:118, and tone ('Mafeni (1969; 1972), Idudhe (1990, 2001) assert that Isoko is a tonal language'; Dunstan 1969:119 'terraced-level tone language'; Elugbe/Donwa deny downstep). No statement about Isoko word stress; stress discussed only for English/Nigerian English.

sources.note: Nothing about stress. Uzere Isoko analysed as 'two tones plus final low raising' (all final L raised to mid in statements and citation forms; no downdrift), correcting Mafeni 1969's 'two tones plus downstep'; fn.5: nouns fall into lexical tone groups, verbs do not.

sources.note: Secondary (Ilolo 2013: 22): 'Mafeni (1969; 1972), Idudhe (1990) and (2001) asse[r]t that Isoko is a tonal language.. They claim that there are basically three tones in Isoko: high, low and mid-high or down stepped tones' with the triplet ekpe LL 'leopard' / LH 'peeling' / L-M 'sand' -- i.e. a three-way (H, L, downstepped/mid-high) account that differs from the two-level statement listed here (Donwa-Ifode 1985; Elugbe 1977 treat the third level as predictable final-low raising).
